raw_case_text:
A 71-year-old-man living in the countryside presented to several clinics with the complaint of swelling and redness on the right forehead 5 months ago and received various topical antibiotic treatments. However, lesions did not respond to treatments and spread to the periorbital region, and he was referred to our clinic with a preliminary diagnosis of preseptal cellulitis. On inspection, there were edema and hyperemia on both eyelids on the right side, predominantly on the upper eyelid, and crusted lesions that were mainly located on the lateral aspect of the right eyebrow and spread to the forehead (Fig. 1). There was no heat or tenderness on the eyelids. Bilateral visual acuity was 20/20. The anterior segment and fundus examinations were normal. Eye movements were normal bilaterally. Medical history revealed no trauma, chronic systemic disease, or known immunodeficiency disorder. Orbital computed tomography was reported to be consistent with preseptal cellulitis. The patient was consulted by the dermatology department to rule out herpetic infection and impetigo. Intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam 4 x 2 g was started after consultation with the infectious diseases department. On the 5th day of the treatment, there was no response to the treatment. Thus, the infectious diseases and dermatology departments were consulted again. Infectious diseases started intravenous (iv) amphotericin-B 3 mg/kg for possible fungal infection and it was decided to continue with intravenous (iv) piperacillin-tazobactam 3 x 0.5 g. There was no additional recommendation from the dermatology department. No regression was observed in clinical findings on the 12th day of treatment. Therefore, it was decided to perform a biopsy of the skin lesions.
Histopathological evaluation of the biopsy was reported as cutaneous leishmaniasis. The patient was consulted by the dermatology department again and it was decided to perform an intralesional glucantime injection. Glucantime injection was administered as an intralesional injection once a week for 5 weeks (1 cycle). At the end of this period, regression of the lesions was observed and the treatment was continued for one more cycle. After the second cycle, significant improvement was detected in the lesions (Fig. 2). Following 4 years of treatment, there was no sign of infection and the lesions healed without any scarring (Fig. 3).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 71-year-old rural man presented with a 5-month history of progressive painless erythema, edema, and crusted lesions spreading from his right forehead to his right eyebrow and right upper and lower eyelids.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed redness and swelling on his right forehead 5 months earlier that spread to the right periorbital region despite multiple courses of topical antibiotics. Referred with a preliminary diagnosis of preseptal cellulitis, he failed to improve after 5 days of intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam (2 g QID) and 7 additional days of IV amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/day) plus IV piperacillin-tazobactam (0.5 g TID), prompting a diagnostic skin biopsy on hospital day 12.
subjective.past_medical_history: Rural resident with no history of trauma, chronic systemic illness, or immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for eyelid warmth, tenderness, pain, or visual loss.

objective.physical_examination: Non-tender, non-warm edema and hyperemia of both right eyelids (predominantly the right upper eyelid) accompanied by crusted plaques over the lateral right eyebrow extending onto the right forehead; bilateral visual acuity 20/20, normal extraocular motility, and normal anterior and posterior ocular segments.
objective.advanced_workup: Orbital CT showed soft-tissue changes reported as consistent with preseptal cellulitis. Incisional biopsy histopathology of the right eyebrow/forehead lesion performed on hospital day 12 confirmed cutaneous leishmaniasis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Bacterial preseptal cellulitis, impetigo, herpes zoster/simplex, and deep fungal infection were excluded by lack of response to broad-spectrum antibiotics and amphotericin B and by day-12 skin biopsy histopathology confirming periorbital Cutaneous Leishmaniasis. Treatment with two 5-week cycles of weekly intralesional meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime) injections achieved complete, scar-free resolution of the forehead and eyelid lesions with no recurrence over 4 years of follow-up.
